title: Lyrical Ballads
author: William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge
written: Mostly between March and July 1798, on and around the Quantock Hills, with The Ancyent Marinere begun on a walk in November 1797
setting: The Somerset coast and the Quantocks, the Wye valley above Tintern, and the roads, cottages and commons where the two poets kept meeting people worth listening to
lengthNote: Twenty-three poems in 1798, opening with The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere and closing with Tintern Abbey; the Astor edition adds poems from the 1800 volume
openingLine: It is an ancyent Marinere, And he stoppeth one of three.
summary: Two young poets published this anonymously in 1798 and changed what English poetry was allowed to be about. The subjects are a discharged soldier, a woman whose child has died, an old huntsman who cannot cut through a root, a boy sent for the doctor who spends the night listening to an owl — people who had been comic or invisible in verse. The language is deliberately plain, the metre is borrowed from street ballads, and the book ends with a hundred and sixty lines of blank verse above the Wye that set the terms for the next century of poetry.
referenceStyle: poem title, and line numbers where the poem is long enough to need them

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of Lyrical Ballads, With a Few Other Poems (eBook 9622)
sourceText.note: The 1798 first edition, with Coleridge's original spelling of the Ancyent Marinere. The Astor edition also prints poems added in 1800; the quotations here are all from the 1798 texts.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Anonymously, by Joseph Cottle in Bristol, in an edition of five hundred. Neither poet's name appeared on it.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: In the year the two men lived four miles apart in Somerset and walked most days.

atAGlance.label: Contents
atAGlance.note: Four by Coleridge, the rest by Wordsworth, opening with the Marinere and closing above Tintern Abbey.

atAGlance.label: The claim
atAGlance.note: The Advertisement offers the poems as trials of whether ordinary speech can carry poetry.

structure.label: The Advertisement and the Marinere
structure.title: A warning to the reader, and a ghost ship
structure.summary: The book opens by telling its readers that they may not think these are poems at all, and then hands them the strangest thing in it. Coleridge's Marinere is in archaic spelling and ballad stanzas, and it takes up nearly a quarter of the volume — a supernatural sea voyage placed at the front of a book that is otherwise about Somerset paupers.

scenes.title: Experiments
scenes.summary: The poems are offered as trials of whether the language of ordinary conversation can be used for poetry, with a warning that readers will have to set their usual expectations aside.

scenes.ref: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
scenes.title: The albatross
scenes.summary: A wedding guest is held by an old sailor who shot a bird, watched his crew die, and cannot stop telling anyone about it.

scenes.ref: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
scenes.title: The becalmed sea
scenes.summary: Thirst, rotting decks and a painted ship: the stretch of the poem everybody remembers, and the one Coleridge's contemporaries found absurd.

structure.label: The talking poems
structure.title: Plain words, awkward metre, real people
structure.summary: Wordsworth's contribution begins with poems that sound like someone telling you a story at a gate. The diction is deliberately flat, the narrators are unreliable or obtuse, and the incidents are so slight that reviewers thought the book a joke. The Thorn is narrated by a garrulous retired sea captain; The Idiot Boy spends four hundred lines on a boy who is never in any danger.

scenes.title: A curse that works
scenes.summary: An old woman gathers sticks from a hedge, a young farmer catches her, and her prayer leaves him cold for the rest of his life.

scenes.title: The root
scenes.summary: An old huntsman cannot cut through a root; the poet does it in one blow, and the gratitude he gets makes him more uncomfortable than ingratitude would.

scenes.title: Three feet long, and two feet wide
scenes.summary: A narrator who cannot stop measuring things tells, or half tells, the story of Martha Ray and her child.

scenes.title: The owl and the moon
scenes.summary: Betty Foy sends her son for the doctor; the comedy is real, and so is the tenderness, and Wordsworth defended the poem for the rest of his life.

structure.label: The dispossessed
structure.title: Children who will not be corrected, and the people on the road
structure.summary: A cluster of poems about people who have lost something and will not be talked out of the loss: a girl who counts her dead siblings among the living, a shepherd down to his last sheep, a mother without a home. They are the most political poems in the book, and none of them argues.

scenes.title: The arithmetic
scenes.summary: An adult explains twice that two of the children are dead, and the little girl declines to change her answer.

scenes.title: How to make a child lie
scenes.summary: A father presses his son for a reason and gets an invented one, and the poem's subtitle calls it a lesson in teaching falsehood.

scenes.title: Fifty sheep to one
scenes.summary: A man weeps in a public road over the last of the flock he has sold, one by one, to feed his children.

scenes.title: War and the parish
scenes.summary: A woman's account of eviction, an army camp and destitution, in Spenserian stanzas that predate the rest of the book.

structure.label: The arguing poems
structure.title: Books, woods, and what teaches
structure.summary: Two short poems in dialogue set out the book's position more baldly than the Advertisement dares: reading is not the only way of learning, and dissection destroys what it examines. They are quotable to the point of being misquoted, and they are the reason the volume is treated as a manifesto.

scenes.title: On a grey stone
scenes.summary: Matthew asks why the poet is sitting idle instead of reading, and gets an answer about the mind's passive powers.

scenes.title: One impulse from a vernal wood
scenes.summary: The reply, with the book closed: nature as teacher, and the famous charge that analysis murders its subject.

scenes.title: What man has made of man
scenes.summary: Pleasure in a grove and grief at human arrangements, held in the same short poem.

structure.label: Tintern Abbey
structure.title: Five years, and a sister on the bank
structure.summary: The last poem in the volume is unlike everything before it: unrhymed, unhurried, and built out of one long act of remembering. Wordsworth composed it in his head walking back to Bristol and wrote nothing down until he arrived. It states the whole Romantic argument about memory, landscape and consolation, and then hands it to his sister as insurance.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: Five summers on, the same cliffs, the same hedge-rows, and a mind checking itself against a remembered place.

scenes.title: The compensation
scenes.summary: What is lost with youth is replaced by the still, sad music of humanity and a sense of something deeply interfused.

scenes.title: The address to Dorothy
scenes.summary: He turns to his sister and asks her to carry the memory for him, which turns a poem about time into a poem about someone else.

characters.name: The Ancyent Marinere
characters.role: The sailor who stops the wedding guest
characters.summary: He shot a bird for no reason he can name and has been explaining it ever since. The poem gives him a punishment with no proportion to the crime and a moral at the end that does not cover what happened, which is why readers have argued about him for two hundred years.
characters.clue: Holds a wedding guest with his eye, and cannot finish being sorry.
characters.firstAppearance: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere

characters.name: The Wedding Guest
characters.role: The listener, kept from the feast
characters.summary: He is late, he is unwilling, and he is changed by the end. His resistance is the poem's measure of the tale's force, and his final state — a sadder and a wiser man — is the closest thing the volume has to a statement about what listening to other people costs.
characters.clue: Beats his breast, hears the bassoon, and cannot leave.
characters.firstAppearance: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere

characters.name: Martha Ray
characters.summary: She sits on the mountain in a scarlet cloak crying oh misery, and the poem never establishes what happened to her child. Wordsworth gives the story to a narrator who cannot tell it, so the reader is left doing what the village does: assembling a woman's tragedy out of gossip and a measured pond.
characters.clue: Named in a poem that will not say what she did.

characters.name: The narrator of The Thorn
characters.role: A retired sea captain with time on his hands
characters.summary: Wordsworth's note describes him as a man of slow faculties and deep feelings who has settled in a village where he knows nobody. He measures the pond, repeats himself, and passes on what he has heard, and the poem's subject turns out to be his way of telling rather than the events.
characters.clue: Has measured the pond: three feet long, and two feet wide.

characters.name: The little maid
characters.role: The eight-year-old of We are seven
characters.summary: She lives in a churchyard cottage with two of her siblings buried twelve steps from the door, and counts them in. The adult questioner repeats the arithmetic three times and gets nowhere, and the poem ends with his failure rather than her correction.
characters.clue: Answers an argument about death with the word still.

characters.name: The questioner
characters.role: The adult voice in the child poems
characters.summary: He appears in We are seven and in Anecdote for Fathers, and in both he is the one who comes off worse. Wordsworth uses him to put the reader's own reasonableness in the poem and let it be defeated by a child who is not arguing at all.
characters.clue: Presses a child for a reason twice, and is taught something both times.

characters.name: Betty Foy
characters.role: The mother of the idiot boy
characters.summary: She sends her son out at night for a doctor and then spends the poem in an agony of self-reproach looking for him. Wordsworth insisted for the rest of his life that the poem was written in love rather than condescension, and the writing bears him out: her panic is given the same attention a heroine's would be.
characters.clue: Loses her son to an owl and a moon, and finds him where she left the pony.

characters.name: Johnny Foy
characters.role: The boy sent for the doctor
characters.summary: He never reaches the doctor and comes home with a report of the night that is pure sensation: cocks crowing, a cold sun, the moon. His account is the only piece of poetry produced inside the poem, which is the joke and the argument together.
characters.clue: Says the cocks crowed to-whoo, and that the sun shone cold.

characters.name: The sister above the Wye
characters.role: The listener of Tintern Abbey, addressed in the last fifty lines
characters.summary: She is silent throughout and is given the poem's whole argument to keep. Wordsworth turns from his own loss to her present pleasure, predicts her future grief, and asks her to remember that he stood there — which makes memory a thing two people hold rather than one.
characters.clue: Has wild eyes, and is told what she will need when the poet is gone.

relationships.label: sister of, and entrusted with the memory

characters.name: The poet
characters.role: The first-person voice of the Wordsworth poems
characters.summary: He walks, listens, asks the wrong questions and reports what he could not get. Across the volume he is a man being taught by the people he meets and by the places he returns to, and the last poem turns him from a collector of other people's stories into the subject of one.
characters.clue: Cuts through the root Simon Lee cannot, and is embarrassed by the thanks.

relationships.label: brother of, and gives the poem to

themes.name: The language really used by men
themes.summary: The Advertisement puts the whole book forward as an experiment in whether ordinary conversation can carry poetry. In practice that means short words, flat statements, a good deal of repetition, and reviewers who complained that they had been sent prose.
themes.development: The 1798 poems try it on tramps, farmers and children; by 1800 Wordsworth had written a preface to defend what he had done, and by 1817 Coleridge had written a chapter to say it could not be done at all.

themes.name: What a wood can teach
themes.summary: Nature in this volume is not scenery. It is a source of instruction that the poems set directly against books, sermons and analysis, and it is credited with the moral education the schoolroom claims.
themes.development: Stated as a joke against study in The Tables Turned, complicated in Lines written in early spring, and turned into something far stranger in Tintern Abbey, where the teacher is a presence the poet cannot name.

themes.name: Five years, and the mind checking itself
themes.summary: The book's last poem makes remembering an activity rather than a mood: a man measures his present feeling against a five-year-old one and finds the loss and the compensation in the same landscape.
themes.development: Memory is a burden in the Marinere, a comfort in Tintern Abbey, and in both cases something that has to be told to another person before it can be borne.

themes.name: The people in the road
themes.summary: Discharged soldiers, evicted tenants, shepherds selling their last sheep, old women gathering sticks from a hedge. Poetry had used such figures for pathos or comedy; this book gives them the grammar of the poem and lets them speak first.
themes.development: The 1798 poems report the poor without moralising; the war, the enclosures and the parish system are visible in the background of nearly every one and are never named as causes.

themes.name: Reading against looking
themes.summary: Two poems stage a straight argument about how a person learns, and the book's most quoted line accuses science of killing what it examines. The position is more careful than the slogan: the poems attack dissection, not attention.
themes.development: Expostulation and Reply raises it, The Tables Turned pushes it to an extreme, and Tintern Abbey then describes a kind of seeing that is neither idleness nor analysis.

themes.name: People who cannot be reached
themes.summary: A child who will not revise her count, a woman who sits on a mountain saying the same two words, a sailor nobody can help, a man cursed with a cold that no fire touches. The volume keeps arriving at someone who cannot be argued out of their condition.
themes.development: Early poems treat the isolation as a puzzle for the observer; by Tintern Abbey the poet has accepted that the only remedy on offer is another person's presence.

techniques.name: The ballad stanza
techniques.definition: Four-line stanzas alternating four and three stresses, rhyming abcb — the metre of street songs and broadsides.
techniques.inThisBook: Using it for serious poetry was the book's first provocation. Coleridge keeps its archaic furniture and adds to it; Wordsworth strips it down until the metre is carrying a conversation about a dead child.

techniques.name: Lines that come back
techniques.definition: A phrase repeated at intervals, often without change.
techniques.inThisBook: Martha Ray's cry and the thorn's measurements return again and again, so that the poem behaves like the mind of its narrator. The repetition irritated the first reviewers, which was the price of the effect.

techniques.name: Unrhymed pentameter
techniques.definition: Five-stress lines without rhyme, the metre of Milton and of English drama.
techniques.inThisBook: Held back until the last poem. After twenty-two ballads the sentence lengths open out in Tintern Abbey, and the change of metre is the change of subject.

techniques.name: Poems that argue
techniques.definition: A poem built as an exchange between two speakers.
techniques.inThisBook: Expostulation and Reply and The Tables Turned are two halves of one conversation; We are seven and Anecdote for Fathers are arguments the adult loses. Putting the opposition inside the poem keeps the doctrine from becoming a sermon.

techniques.name: Speaking to someone in the poem
techniques.definition: Turning from the reader to a named listener inside the text.
techniques.inThisBook: The Marinere fixes the wedding guest; Tintern Abbey turns to a sister who never speaks. Both poems need a listener present, so that the reader is watching someone else being told.

techniques.name: Places given exactly
techniques.definition: Naming and describing real ground rather than generic scenery.
techniques.inThisBook: Hedge-rows run wild, the smoke rises from among the trees, the thorn stands a certain number of paces from a pond. The precision is what makes the argument about nature something other than a preference.

techniques.name: Telling it afterwards
techniques.definition: A narrator recounting events that are already over, with the ending known.
techniques.inThisBook: Almost every poem here is a report: the Marinere's voyage, the vagrant's ruin, the huntsman's better days. The distance between the event and the telling is where the feeling collects.

quotations.text: The majority of the following poems are to be considered as experiments.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the unsigned note that introduces the 1798 volume.
quotations.analysis: A word borrowed from the laboratory, at a moment when poetry was still expected to be an art of finish. It sets up the reader to judge by results rather than by decorum, and it is the first sign that the book intends an argument as well as a collection.

quotations.text: It is an ancyent Marinere, And he stoppeth one of three.
quotations.reference: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere, 1-2
quotations.context: The first lines of the book.
quotations.analysis: Archaic spelling, ballad metre and a man seizing a stranger, all in fourteen words. Coleridge is announcing an old form on purpose; the volume that claims to use ordinary speech opens in a language nobody had spoken for two hundred years.

quotations.text: With my cross bow I shot the Albatross.
quotations.reference: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
quotations.context: The end of the first part, after the bird has followed the ship for nine days.
quotations.analysis: The crime is reported in a single line with no motive attached, and the poem never supplies one. Everything that follows is disproportionate to it, which is the point: the Marinere's world runs on a scale of consequence that no explanation will fit.

quotations.text: Water, water, every where, Ne any drop to drink.
quotations.reference: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
quotations.context: The becalmed ship on a rotting sea.
quotations.analysis: The 1798 spelling keeps the archaic 'ne', which later editions dropped, and the line is better for the awkwardness: the ballad is pretending to be older than it is. The image survives in ordinary speech, usually misquoted, which is a fair measure of the poem's reach.

quotations.text: Oh! what’s the matter? what’s the matter?
quotations.context: The opening of the poem about a farmer who catches an old woman taking sticks.
quotations.analysis: A poem that begins with a question a neighbour would ask over a wall. Wordsworth took the incident from a medical book and put it in ballad metre, and the effect is a case study told in the voice of village gossip.

quotations.text: I’ve measured it from side to side: ’Tis three feet long, and two feet wide.
quotations.context: The narrator describing the pond beside the thorn.
quotations.analysis: The most mocked couplet of the age, and entirely deliberate: a man who cannot tell a story reaches for the only certainty he has, a tape measure. Wordsworth cut the lines in 1820 under pressure, which is the clearest evidence of how far the experiment had gone.

quotations.text: The cocks did crow to-whoo, to-whoo, And the sun did shine so cold.
quotations.context: Johnny's entire account of his night, given at the end of the poem.
quotations.analysis: Four hundred lines of a mother's terror resolve into two lines of synaesthesia from the boy everyone in the poem has been worrying about. It is the volume's boldest claim: the imagination it has been arguing for turns up in the character the reader was invited to pity.

quotations.text: A simple child, dear brother Jim
quotations.context: The first line of the poem, in its 1798 form.
quotations.analysis: The address to 'brother Jim' was dropped from later editions, and with it the sense of a poem begun in the middle of a conversation. Keeping the 1798 reading shows how casual the opening was meant to sound before the argument starts.

quotations.context: The last line of the poem, after the adult has explained twice that two of the children are dead.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends with the child unmoved and the adult out of arguments, and Wordsworth gives her the final word rather than a moral. What looks like a poem about a child's confusion is a poem about an adult's certainty failing in the open.

quotations.text: Why William, on that old grey stone
quotations.context: Matthew opening the argument, finding the poet sitting and doing nothing.
quotations.analysis: The objection is given first and given a name. By letting the sensible position speak in its own voice, the poem earns the reply it is about to make, and the pair becomes a debate rather than a lecture.

quotations.text: Think you, mid all this mighty sum Of things for ever speaking, That nothing of itself will come, But we must still be seeking?
quotations.analysis: The case for what he calls a wise passiveness, put as a question rather than a claim. 'Things for ever speaking' gives the world the active part and the mind the receptive one, which reverses the usual account of attention.

quotations.text: Up! up! my friend, and clear your looks
quotations.context: The reply poem, ordering Matthew away from his books.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation marks do real work: the poem's argument is about energy, and it starts by sounding like someone pulling a friend out of a chair. The doctrine that follows is only tolerable because it arrives in this voice.

quotations.text: One impulse from a vernal wood May teach you more of man, Of moral evil and of good, Than all the sages can.
quotations.context: The middle of the poem, at its most provocative.
quotations.analysis: The claim is deliberately excessive — more than all the sages — and that excess has been quoted against Wordsworth ever since. Read in the argument it belongs to, it is a move in a debate, not a position paper.

quotations.context: The end of the stanza about science and art.
quotations.analysis: Four words that have outlived their poem. The charge is not against knowledge but against a method that takes a living thing apart to describe it, and the volume's own practice — watching people closely without explaining them — is the alternative on offer.

quotations.text: Five years have passed; five summers, with the length Of five long winters!
quotations.context: The opening of the last poem in the volume.
quotations.analysis: The same span counted three ways, each slower than the last, so that the line performs the passage it reports. After twenty-two ballads the ear notices at once that the rhyme has gone and the sentences have stopped stopping every fourth line.

quotations.text: sensations sweet, Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart
quotations.context: Describing what the remembered landscape has done for him in the years away.
quotations.analysis: The claim is physiological, not sentimental: a memory of a place is described as something circulating in the body. It is the volume's clearest statement that feeling is a kind of evidence.

quotations.text: The still, sad music of humanity
quotations.context: Accounting for what maturity has given him in place of youth's raw pleasure.
quotations.analysis: The compensation is other people's suffering, heard rather than witnessed. The phrase quietly justifies the rest of the book: the vagrants, huntsmen and mothers of the preceding poems are the music he means.

quotations.text: a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused
quotations.context: The poem's central and most careful passage.
quotations.analysis: Everything here is held at arm's length — a sense, something, far more deeply — because naming it would commit him to a doctrine. The vagueness is exact: this is a man describing an experience he trusts and cannot define.

quotations.text: Nature never did betray The heart that loved her
quotations.context: Turning to his sister, and telling her what will hold when the rest does not.
quotations.analysis: A promise made to somebody else, at the point where the poet has stopped trusting his own future. Read beside the Marinere's voyage at the other end of the book, the assurance looks less like a doctrine than a hope stated out loud.

timeline.label: Wordsworth and Coleridge meet
timeline.detail: Introduced in Bristol; within two years they were living four miles apart in Somerset.

timeline.label: The Quantock year begins
timeline.detail: The Wordsworths take Alfoxden House, a walk from Coleridge's cottage at Nether Stowey. Most of the book is written in the twelve months that follow.

timeline.label: The Marinere begun on a walk
timeline.detail: Planned in November on a walk towards Lynton, partly to pay for the trip; a friend's dream of a skeleton ship and a sailor's account of albatrosses went into it.

timeline.label: Tintern Abbey composed
timeline.detail: Written in July, in Wordsworth's head, on the walk back to Bristol from the Wye, and set down on arrival.

timeline.label: Published anonymously
timeline.detail: Joseph Cottle issues five hundred copies in Bristol in September with neither poet named.

timeline.label: Southey reviews it
timeline.detail: In the Critical Review he calls the Marinere a Dutch attempt at German sublimity, and the volume's best-known poem is written off at once.

timeline.label: Germany
timeline.detail: The two poets leave for Goslar and Ratzeburg; the separation ends the year of daily collaboration.

timeline.label: The second edition
timeline.detail: Two volumes, Wordsworth's name alone on the title page, Michael and the Lucy poems added, the Marinere respelled and moved out of first place.

timeline.label: The Preface expanded
timeline.detail: Wordsworth adds the definitions the book is now remembered by, including poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings.

timeline.label: Coleridge answers back
timeline.detail: Biographia Literaria devotes two chapters to disputing Wordsworth's theory of poetic diction while praising the poems it produced.

timeline.label: The measurements go
timeline.detail: Wordsworth finally cuts the three-feet-long couplet from The Thorn after twenty years of ridicule.

places.name: Alfoxden House, Holford
places.note: The house the Wordsworths rented in 1797-98; most of Wordsworth's contributions were written here.

places.name: Nether Stowey
places.note: Coleridge's cottage, four miles across the hills.

places.name: Tintern, Monmouthshire
places.note: The abbey a few miles below the spot on the Wye where the last poem is set.

places.name: Bristol
places.note: Joseph Cottle's shop, where the book was printed and published in 1798.

places.name: Lynton, north Devon
places.note: The direction of the November walk on which The Ancyent Marinere was planned.

places.name: Goslar, Lower Saxony
places.note: Where Wordsworth spent the winter after publication, writing the poems that filled the 1800 edition.

criticalViews.summary: The standard account treats 1798 as a break: ordinary subjects, plain diction, feeling as authority, and the end of eighteenth-century poetic decorum.
criticalViews.counter: The book sold slowly and anonymously, its manifesto was written two years later, and much of it belongs to a ballad revival already twenty years old. The break is clearer in hindsight than it was at the time.

criticalViews.position: An experiment in the real language of men
criticalViews.summary: Wordsworth's claim, made in the Advertisement and expanded in the Preface, is that there is no essential difference between the language of poetry and that of good prose.
criticalViews.counter: Coleridge devoted a chapter of Biographia Literaria to showing that his friend's best lines are not in any ordinary man's language, and that where they are, the poems are weakest.

criticalViews.position: The Marinere does not belong in it
criticalViews.summary: Wordsworth blamed the poem for the volume's poor sale, said it had great defects, and moved it out of first place in 1800.
criticalViews.counter: It is the piece everyone can still quote, and the book's argument about isolation and compulsive telling runs straight from it into the poems about the poor.

essayQuestions.question: How successfully does the volume use ordinary speech for poetry?
essayQuestions.focus: Diction, metre and the claim of the Advertisement
plan: Start with the Advertisement's word: experiments, and what it asks a reader to suspend.
Take The Thorn's measurements as the extreme case, and account for the ridicule they drew.
Set Simon Lee or We are seven beside it, where the flat language works.
Bring in Coleridge's objection from Biographia Literaria, and test it on a passage of Tintern Abbey.
Conclude on whether the experiment succeeds as theory, as practice, or only in particular poems.

essayQuestions.question: What is Tintern Abbey doing at the end of the book?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, metre and the turn to memory
plan: Describe what changes: blank verse, longer sentences, a single continuous voice.
Trace the poem's three times — the boy, the man five years ago, the man now.
Examine the compensation offered in place of youth, and the phrase about the music of humanity.
Account for the turn to the sister, and what entrusting the memory to her achieves.
Argue for what the volume gains by ending here rather than on another ballad.

essayQuestions.question: How does the book present the rural poor?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, sympathy and the refusal to moralise
plan: Collect the cases: the female vagrant, the last of the flock, Simon Lee, Goody Blake.
Note what the poems withhold: causes, blame, and any call to action.
Consider the effect of giving these figures direct speech and the poem's own metre.
Weigh the charge of condescension, using The Idiot Boy and Wordsworth's defence of it.
Decide whether attention without argument is a political position.

essayQuestions.question: Does The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere fit the volume it opens?
essayQuestions.focus: The two poets and one book
plan: Set out the contrast: archaic spelling and supernatural machinery against Somerset paupers in plain words.
Show what the two halves share — compulsive telling, a listener who cannot leave, a punishment out of proportion.
Use Wordsworth's own complaints and the 1800 demotion as evidence of the strain.
Consider Coleridge's account of the division of labour between them.
Conclude on whether the volume is one book or two bound together.

discussionQuestions: The Advertisement warns readers they may feel awkwardness and struggle. Which poem still produces that, and is the discomfort doing something?
Is We are seven about a child's misunderstanding or an adult's?
The Tables Turned says we murder to dissect. What would that mean for the study of this poem?
Why does Wordsworth give the poem's last fifty lines to a sister who never speaks?
The Thorn's narrator cannot tell the story. What do you learn from a poem told by the wrong person?
If you had bought this book in 1798 with no name on the title page, what would you have thought you had?

related.why: The poem that opens this volume, printed on its own with the 1798 text and its later revisions.
What Coleridge wrote either side of the Quantock year, including the conversation poems.
Written twenty years later by a reader of both poets, and it quotes the Marinere at the moment its narrator loses his nerve.
Published in 1811, and unsparing about the fashion for feeling that this book helped to license.
The blank verse Wordsworth is answering in Tintern Abbey, and the measure of what he does differently with it.
